body: Nine declared ingredients: Tribulus terrestris, tongkat ali (Eurycoma longifolia), Epimedium as a genus, Fadogia agrestis, sarsaparilla, damiana (Turnera diffusa), pine pollen, ginseng and piperine.
Eight of those are plants and the ninth is a compound taken out of pepper. Four of the nine names do not identify a species, and the cards below say which four.
Two capsules with breakfast, and at least 1 litre of water across the day.
Two a day is the serving and the ceiling with it. Fifty capsules at 800 mg come to 25 days, which is £1.60 a day.
Not printed on the listing. Dry, out of direct sun and lid on is what we would do with any capsule. No fridge.
The listing states that this jar is for men only. It gives no reason for that and we are not going to supply one.

If you take nitrates, blood pressure medication, heart medication or anything else on prescription, speak to your GP or pharmacist first: piperine is well known to change how the body takes up and clears some medications. Not for children, and not in pregnancy or while breastfeeding. Pine pollen is a pollen, so anyone who reacts to pollen should leave this one alone.
Sent out from 599 Smithdown Road, Liverpool, Tuesday to Sunday. UK delivery is free over £50, or you can collect from the shop between 10 and 6, any day except Monday.

ingredients.intro: In the order the listing declares them. Eight are plants and the ninth is a compound taken out of one. Four of the nine names identify a species; the other four are common names or a genus, and those cards say so rather than choosing a plant on the label's behalf. Where a name does not identify a species we have left the frame empty, because a photograph would be picking one.

cards.alt: A low spreading tribulus plant with small yellow flowers and spined fruit on dry ground
cards.p: A low annual of the Zygophyllaceae that runs flat over hot dry ground from the Mediterranean through South Asia into Africa and Australia. The fruit splits into hard spined nutlets, which is where the English names come from. The listing spells the second word with one r missing. It does not say which part of the plant is used.

cards.alt: A slender tongkat ali tree with long pinnate leaves in lowland forest
cards.p: The listing gives the Malay name. It belongs to a slender understorey tree of the Simaroubaceae in the lowland forests of Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Vietnam, thin enough at full height to be taken for a sapling. The root is the part that reaches the trade. The listing does not say which part is in the capsule.

A genus of woodland perennials in the Berberidaceae, most of them Chinese, with thin leathery leaves and spurred flowers. A genus is not an ingredient: this one holds dozens of species. Neither the species nor the part used is printed, so the frame stays empty.
cards.none: of a species the label does not name

cards.p: A small shrub of the Rubiaceae from the savanna belt of West Africa, from Nigeria eastwards. The dried stem is what is sold under the name. The listing spells it agrestris; the accepted binomial is Fadogia agrestis. We found no photograph of the plant we could use, so this frame is empty as well.
cards.none: of this plant that we could use

cards.p: A trade name rather than a species. It covers several climbers in the genus Smilax, and is also used for Hemidesmus indicus in India and Aralia nudicaulis in North America. The root is what the word points at in all of them. With no binomial on the label there is no way to say which plant is in the jar.
cards.none: of a species the label does not name

cards.alt: A small damiana shrub with toothed leaves and a yellow flower
cards.p: A small aromatic shrub of the Passifloraceae, native to Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and southern Texas, with toothed leaves and a small yellow flower. The leaf is the part in trade. The listing prints the common name only; the binomial above is the accepted one for it.

Pollen shed by the male cones of pine trees and collected in spring. Pinus runs to over a hundred species and the listing does not say which one, or where it was gathered. It is also the one ingredient here that is a pollen, which matters to anyone who reacts to them.
cards.none: of a species the label does not name

cards.p: Another common name doing a binomial's work. Ginseng usually means Panax ginseng from Korea and northeast China, sometimes Panax quinquefolius from North America, and on some labels Eleutherococcus senticosus, a different plant in the same family. The root is what is sold under all three. The shop sells a ginseng of its own, and this listing does not say whether it is the same plant.
cards.none: of a species the label does not name

cards.alt: Green peppercorn spikes on a black ground
cards.p: The one ingredient here that is not a plant or a part of one. Piperine is a compound taken out of pepper, the fruit of Piper nigrum, which is why this card shows peppercorns rather than the ingredient itself. It is also the reason for the line about prescriptions on the sheet below.

doctrine.h3: We publish the specification. We do not publish claims about what it does.
doctrine.p: This jar prints its list, so this page prints it back: in Latin where the label gives a binomial, and in plain English where it does not. Four of the nine names do not identify a species, and those rows say so rather than choosing a plant for you. What the formula is for is not on this page and neither is any reading of the name on the front.

spec.intro: Nine ingredients: four names that identify a species, four that do not, one that names a compound, and the figures the listing does not give.

reiss.label: From Reiss
reiss.h2: Nine names, and four of them are not species
paras: A list is better than no list, and this jar has one, which already puts it ahead of half the formulas on my own shelf. Then you read it slowly. Sarsaparilla, ginseng, pine pollen, epimedium: four names that each cover more than one plant, and in two cases plants from different families. A name that covers three plants is not an ingredient, it is a category.

The other four are species and I have printed them in Latin above, spelling corrected in two places where the listing has a letter missing. Not one of the nine says which part of the plant is in the capsule. Root, leaf, stem and pollen are what the trade usually sells under these names, and usually is not a specification.

The ninth is not a plant at all. Piperine is a compound taken out of pepper, and it is the reason there is a line about prescriptions on the sheet. Anything that changes how the body takes up a medication belongs in the safety row of a page, printed plainly, whether or not it helps me sell the jar.

The listing also says this one is for men only. I have printed that because the label prints it, and I have not printed a reason, because the label does not give one and the reason would be mine rather than the manufacturer's. If you want to know more before you buy, the counter is the place for that conversation.
reiss.pull: A name that covers three plants is not an ingredient, it is a category.
